issues.legal_issue: A decision on proprietary title made in proceedings before a revenue court does not bar a later civil suit when that court was not competent to try the later suit.
material_facts: A revenue-court suit sought a co-sharer’s share of village profits, and a dispute about proprietary title was referred to a civil court for determination under the governing tenancy law.
The revenue court entered a decree based on that determination.
The later suit sought a declaration of title to properties and an injunction, relief not provided for by the revenue-court suit identified in the tenancy law.
The revenue court was not competent to try the later civil suit.
issues.conclusion: The prior revenue-court decision did not operate as res judicata in the later civil suit, which was maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 requires the court deciding the former suit to be competent to try the subsequent suit. Since the later suit was not within the revenue court’s exclusive jurisdiction under sections 227 and 230 of the Agra Tenancy Act, 1926, and that court could not try it, the required competence was absent. Section 271 of that Act provided for a civil court to decide a referred issue of proprietary title, after which the revenue court decided the revenue suit. The Court approved Venkatarama Rao v. Venkayya, A.I.R. 1954 Mad. 788.

predicates.subsequent_civil_title_suit: A party later brought a civil suit seeking a declaration of title or related relief.
predicates.prior_revenue_profit_suit: An earlier revenue-court proceeding sought a co-sharer’s share of profits, and the court decided it after a title issue was referred for determination.
predicates.prior_court_lacked_competence_to_try_lat: The court deciding the earlier proceeding was not competent to try the kind of suit later brought.

issues.definition: When a later civil title suit follows a revenue-court profit proceeding and the earlier court could not try the later kind of suit, the earlier decision does not bar the later suit as res judicata.

issues.legal_issue: A presumption that a Hindu family is joint can be rebutted by evidence of partition, including a prolonged course of conduct showing separation.
material_facts: The family’s ancestral property was limited and yielded little income.
A family member left the ancestral home, entered service, and later began a separate business using his savings.
Family members lived and earned separately, and different members’ names were recorded against portions of ancestral property.
Two brothers were acknowledged to be separate from the appellant, and there was no dispute over the separate enjoyment of income from the ancestral property.
The parties’ conduct over about fifty years was consistent with separation rather than joint status, despite limited contemporaneous evidence of the old transactions.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the finding that the larger family had partitioned during the lifetime of the earlier family member.
issues.legal_principle: A Hindu family is presumed joint until the contrary is proved, but the presumption can be rebutted by direct evidence or a course of conduct. There is no presumption that the remaining members stay united when one member separates; that is decided on the facts. For old transactions where documents and witnesses are unavailable, reasonable inferences may more readily fill evidentiary gaps, though the burden remains on the person asserting partition.

predicates.family_partition_dispute: A party in a dispute over family property asserted that the family had divided.
predicates.prolonged_separate_conduct: Family members acted over a substantial period in ways consistent with separation rather than continuing joint status.
predicates.separate_livelihoods_or_property_records: Family members maintained separate livelihoods or property records reflected separate interests in family property.

issues.definition: In a dispute over family partition, prolonged conduct showing separate lives or property interests establishes partition when it is consistent with separation.

issues.legal_issue: After partition, reunion as a joint Hindu family must be proved by evidence showing an agreement and an intention to resume joint status.
material_facts: The Court found that the larger family had partitioned.
The appellant relied on the uncle and nephews living and working together and acquiring property jointly as evidence of reunion.
The uncle supplied the business capital from his own savings, and the documents generally did not describe the parties as members of a joint Hindu family.
The uncle’s adoption document and will described his properties as self-acquired, and the widow’s name was entered in revenue records for her deceased husband’s share.
The alleged evidence of joint status was ambiguous or self-serving, and the conduct over about fifty years did not establish a conscious agreement to reunite.
issues.conclusion: The Court found that no reunion between the uncle and his nephews, or between the two brothers after the uncle’s death, had been established.
issues.legal_principle: A reunion after partition is presumed against, must be strictly proved, and requires an agreement—express or implied—to reunite in estate and interest with the intention of returning to joint-family status. An express agreement is unnecessary, but conduct must be clear and incapable of explanation on another footing; ambiguous conduct consistent with ordinary joint enjoyment is insufficient. The Court relied on Palani Ammal v. Muthuvenkatacharla Maniagar, (1924) 52 I.A. 83, Venkataramayya v. Tatayya, A.I.R. 1943 Mad. 538, and Ramadin v. Gokul Prasad, A.I.R. 1959 M.P. 251.

predicates.reunion_claim_after_partition: A party claimed that family members who had partitioned later reunited.
predicates.joint_living_or_business: The alleged reunited members lived together, worked together, or acquired property together.
predicates.no_clear_evidence_of_agreement_to_resume: The evidence did not clearly show that the members agreed and intended to resume joint-family status.

issues.definition: When reunion is claimed after partition, shared living or business does not establish reunion without clear evidence of an agreement and intention to resume joint status.

issues.legal_issue: Members of different branches cannot create a subordinate joint Hindu family merely by jointly acquiring property, so their rights in the acquisition do not arise by joint-family survivorship.
material_facts: The uncle and his two nephews belonged to different branches of the larger family.
They acquired properties jointly, but the Court found no reunion between them.
The acquisitions were made without joint-family property being brought into the business or acquisitions.
The appellant claimed the properties as joint-family property and claimed survivorship upon the deaths of the other holders.
issues.conclusion: The joint acquisitions were not joint-family property; the parties held them as co-sharers, their rights were governed by the agreement under which they acquired the properties, and the properties passed by inheritance rather than by survivorship.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara Hindu law, the family or a complete branch or sub-branch can act as a corporate unit capable of holding joint-family property; some members of different branches, or only some members of a single branch, cannot form such a unit. The principle of joint tenancy is unknown to Hindu law except for joint property of an undivided Mitakshara family, which passes by survivorship. The Court relied on Sudarsanam Maistri v. Narasimhulu Maistri, (1902) I.L.R. 25 Mad. 149; Chakra Kannan v. Kunhi Pokker, (1916) I.L.R. 39 Mad. 317; The Official Assignee v. Neelambal Ammal, (1933) 65 M.L.J. 798; Himmat Bahadur v. Bhawani Kunwar, (1908) I.L.R. 30 All. 352; Jogeshwar Narain Deo v. Ram Chund Dutt, (1896) L.R. 23 I.A. 37; and Babu Rani v. Rajendra Baksh Singh, (1933) L.R. 60 I.A. 95. It overruled Sham Narain v. The Court of Wards (1873) 20 W.R. 197 and distinguished Nathu Lal v. Babu Ram, (1936) L.R. 63 I.A. 155, and Ramprashad Tewarry v. Sheachuran Doss, (1866) 10 M.I.A. 490.

predicates.joint_acquisition_dispute: A party claimed that property acquired jointly by family members was joint-family property.
predicates.acquirers_from_different_family_branches: The people who acquired the property together belonged to different branches of the larger family rather than constituting the whole family or a whole branch.
predicates.no_reunion_established: The people who acquired the property together had not been proved to have reunited as a joint Hindu family.

issues.definition: When people from different family branches jointly acquire property without establishing reunion, the acquisition is not joint-family property.
